findings.where: First screen, the hero's sub-line under the heading (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The line the visitor reads next to the only button relies on a size claim, 'Over 40 years of international infrastructure experience'. The house trust rules name exactly this kind of claim as the one to avoid. The checkable fact in the same sentence, a former Lead Lawyer in the World Bank's PPP Group, has to share its weight with that claim.
findings.who_objects: A procurement officer at a development bank judges consultants against terms of reference on the kind of project, the body and the region, so a years count tells them nothing they can check. Mark's own brief asks for confidence without big-firm claims, and the claim pulls against that.

findings.where: First screen, the heading and the sub-line together
findings.fault: The 5-second test only half passes. The first screen says what Mark does, but not who it is for (development banks, agencies, governments) or where he works: 'international' is the only hint of place. A bank's staff member can't see straight away that he works for organisations like theirs, in their region.
findings.who_objects: Staff at multilateral development banks, the named audience, need to see 'done this for bodies like us, in our region' before they write. The page leaves them to infer it.

findings.where: First screen, the hero's heading and sub-line
findings.fault: The headline is a name-and-title label, and the sub-line talks about Mark in the third person ('from a former Lead Lawyer…'). Mark is never heard in his own words on the first screen. The page reads as a firm describing its principal, which is the voice the brand sheet sets aside.
findings.who_objects: Mark: his values ask that he be seen and heard in his own words and that the individual is the brand (§5). The dualite take this direction rests on puts his own words in the headline.

findings.where: First screen, the 'Get in touch' button; the whole page, which has no footer
findings.fault: The only contact route is a mailto button. The email address never appears as text, and there is no footer that carries it, so a visitor whose computer has no mail program set up clicks and gets nothing, or gets a stray app opening. They also have no address they can copy.
findings.who_objects: A visitor on webmail or a locked-down office machine, which is common among agency staff, would hit a dead end at the page's one action. First-visit trust item 7 asks for the address in full as its own link text on every page.

findings.where: Article page specimen, the line under the title ('MMM Infra Blog No. 8 · 18 September 2024')
findings.fault: The article carries no author's name, no one-line bio and no face. Someone arriving on it from a LinkedIn post sees a firm's blog number, not Mark.
findings.who_objects: A reader who lands deep from a shared post can't tell who is speaking or why to trust them (first-visit trust item 12). Mark wants the individual, not the firm, to be the brand.

findings.where: Article page specimen, the lecture link 'Streamlining the PPP Process…' (Lecture · 23 April 2026 · PDF)
findings.fault: The lecture is listed without its venue or the body that invited him, and the label suggests it opens a bare PDF. The most persuasive part of the item, who asked Mark to speak, is missing, and the visitor is sent into a file instead of a page.
findings.who_objects: A procurement reader judges standing by who asked for the work. Without the venue the talk proves little, and a raw PDF gives no route back to Mark or to contacting him (first-visit trust item 4; 'Feel the CV').

findings.where: First screen, the area around the 'Get in touch' button
findings.fault: Nothing outside Mark's own claims stands near the call to action: no named body that published or asked for his work, and no link out to work hosted by such a body. Any added proof must be real; none may be invented.
findings.who_objects: A first-time visitor from a development bank has only self-description to go on before writing. Mark's references to work published by the World Bank or similar bodies are the kind of proof such a reader looks for (first-visit trust item 14).
